title: The Bear Ahead

title: The Running Bear
text: For decades, popular science called Arctodus simus the "running bear."  Some claims said that, despite its bulk,
nxt: it could reach speeds above sixty kilometers per hour in short bursts, chasing down wild horses and young camels.

title: Cracks in the Theory
text: However, as modern studies advanced, cracks began to appear in that picture.
nxt: When researchers compared its limb bones with those of living bears, they found that Arctodus was not as long-legged as it had been thought to be.

title: The Top of the Food Chain
text: For hundreds of thousands of years, the giant short-faced bear may have sat near the top of the food chain across much of North America.

title: The Top of the Food Chain
text: Yet evolution holds a harsh lesson: the larger your body and the narrower your way of life, the more fragile you can be when the world changes.

title: The Top of the Food Chain
text: The very traits that made Arctodus so formidable may have helped doom it.

title: The World Changes
text: About twenty thousand years ago, the Last Glacial Maximum, the coldest stretch of the last Ice Age, began to ebb.
nxt: Over the following millennia, the climate shifted, sometimes quickly.

title: The World Changes
text: The cold, dry grasslands often called the Mammoth Steppe began to break apart.  In many regions, they gave way to forests and wetlands.

title: The World Changes
text: That change may have been bad news for an animal built like Arctodus.  The open landscapes where this wanderer once strode were shrinking.

title: The World Changes
text: In thick forests and muddy bogs, great size and long legs may have become more burden than advantage.
nxt: Moving through dense vegetation takes a lot of energy, and long limbs are awkward on a cluttered forest floor.

nxt: Size and strength are no protection against a rapidly changing world.

title: The Lesson
